----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the fastapi_chameleon library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Setup

Point the library at your Chameleon templates folder once at app startup.


global_init(template_folder: str | ForwardRef('os.PathLike[str]'), auto_reload: bool = False, cache_init: bool = True) -> None

Initialize the Chameleon template engine for your app.

Call this once at startup, pointing it at the folder that holds your ``*.pt``
templates. Template paths used elsewhere (in ``template()``, ``response()``,
``not_found()``, and ``generic_error()``) are resolved relative to this folder.
Call it before the modules that define decorated views are imported, so that
template name inference sees the right folder.

Example::

    from pathlib import Path
    import fastapi_chameleon

    templates = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'templates'
    fastapi_chameleon.global_init(templates, auto_reload=dev_mode)

:param template_folder: Path to the folder containing your Chameleon templates, as a
    ``str`` or any ``os.PathLike`` such as ``pathlib.Path``.
:param bool auto_reload: Reload templates from disk when they change. Handy in
    development; leave ``False`` in production. Defaults to ``False``.
:param bool cache_init: When ``True`` (the default), a second call is a no-op once
    the engine is already initialized. Pass ``False`` to force re-initialization
    (for example, to switch template folders in tests).
:raises FastAPIChameleonException: If ``template_folder`` is empty or is not a directory.


## Rendering views

Decorate FastAPI view functions to render templates, or build a response directly.


template(template_file: Callable[..., ~R] | str | None = None, mimetype: str = 'text/html')

Decorate a FastAPI view to render its return value through a Chameleon template.

Works on both sync and async view functions, and can be used three ways::

    @template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
    @template()                  # infer the template name
    @template                    # bare form, also infers the name

When no template file is given, the name is inferred as ``{module}/{function}``
under the template folder (the module's last dotted segment and the view's name),
preferring a ``.html`` file and falling back to ``.pt``.

The decorated view should return a ``dict`` (used as the template's variables). If
it returns a ``fastapi.Response`` instead, the template is skipped and the response
is passed through unchanged. Returning anything else raises
``FastAPIChameleonException``.

Example::

    @app.get('/')
    @fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
    def index():
        return {'title': 'Home'}

:param template_file: The Chameleon template file (path relative to the template
    folder). Omit it (or pass ``None``) to infer the name from the view. In the bare
    ``@template`` form this argument receives the view function itself.
:param str mimetype: The response media type. Defaults to ``text/html``.
:return: The decorated view (bare form) or a decorator to apply to the view.

response(template_file: str, mimetype: str = 'text/html', status_code: int = 200, **template_data) -> starlette.responses.Response

Render a template and return it as a FastAPI response directly.

Use this when you want a rendered ``Response`` without the ``template()``
decorator, for example to return a fully-formed response from a view that does
its own branching. Requires ``global_init()`` to have been called first.

Example::

    @app.get('/sitemap.xml')
    def sitemap():
        return fastapi_chameleon.response('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml', urls=load_urls())

:param str template_file: The Chameleon template file to render (path relative to
    the template folder, ``*.pt``).
:param str mimetype: The response media type. Defaults to ``text/html``.
:param int status_code: The HTTP status code for the response. Defaults to ``200``.
:param template_data: Keyword arguments passed through to the template as variables.
:return: A ``fastapi.Response`` containing the rendered template, with the given
    media type and status code.
:raises FastAPIChameleonException: If ``global_init()`` has not been called.


## Error responses

Short-circuit a view to render a friendly error page with the right status code.


not_found(four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt') -> NoReturn

Short-circuit the current view and render a friendly 404 page.

Call this from inside a ``template()``-decorated view when a resource cannot be
found. It raises an exception that the decorator catches and turns into an HTTP
404 response rendered from ``four04template_file``. This function never returns
normally.

Example::

    @app.get('/items/{item_id}')
    @fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
    def item(item_id: int):
        item = repo.get(item_id)
        if not item:
            fastapi_chameleon.not_found()
        return {'item': item}

:param str four04template_file: The template to render for the 404 response (path
    relative to the template folder). Defaults to ``errors/404.pt``.
:raises FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: Always; this is how the 404 is signalled
    to the decorator.

generic_error(template_file: str, status_code: int, template_data: dict | None = None) -> NoReturn

Short-circuit the current view and render an error page with a custom status code.

Like ``not_found()``, but for any error: call it from inside a
``template()``-decorated view to render ``template_file`` with the HTTP
``status_code`` you choose (for example ``401`` or ``500``). The decorator catches
the raised exception and builds the response. This function never returns normally.

Example::

    if not user.is_admin:
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})

:param str template_file: The error template to render (path relative to the
    template folder).
:param int status_code: The HTTP status code to return (for example
    ``fastapi.status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED``).
:param dict template_data: Optional variables passed to the template. Defaults to
    ``None`` (an empty context).
:raises FastAPIChameleonGenericException: Always; this is how the error is signalled
    to the decorator.


## Exceptions

Exception types raised by the library (the error helpers raise these internally).


FastAPIChameleonException

Base class for every error raised by fastapi-chameleon.

Raised directly for configuration and rendering problems, such as calling
``global_init()`` with a missing or invalid template folder, rendering before
``global_init()`` has run, or returning an unsupported type from a decorated view.
The control-flow exceptions below subclass it, so catching this type catches them all.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.global_init(settings.template_folder)
    except FastAPIChameleonException as e:
        raise SystemExit(f'Template folder problem: {e}')

FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException(message: str | None = None, four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt')

Signals a 404 response from inside a decorated view.

Raised by ``not_found()`` and caught by the ``template()`` decorator, which renders
``template_file`` with an HTTP 404 status. You normally raise it indirectly via
``not_found()`` rather than constructing it yourself.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found('errors/custom_404.pt')
    except FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException as e:
        assert e.template_file == 'errors/custom_404.pt'

:ivar template_file: The template to render for the 404 response (the constructor
    accepts it as ``four04template_file``).
:vartype template_file: str
:ivar message: The optional human-readable message describing the error.
:vartype message: Optional[str]

FastAPIChameleonGenericException(template_file: str, status_code: int, message: str | None = None, template_data: dict | None = None)

Signals an arbitrary error response from inside a decorated view.

Raised by ``generic_error()`` and caught by the ``template()`` decorator, which
renders ``template_file`` with the chosen ``status_code``. You normally raise it
indirectly via ``generic_error()`` rather than constructing it yourself.

Example::

    try:
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})
    except FastAPIChameleonGenericException as e:
        assert e.status_code == 403 and e.template_data == {'user': user}

:ivar template_file: The template to render for the error response.
:vartype template_file: str
:ivar status_code: The HTTP status code to return.
:vartype status_code: int
:ivar message: The optional human-readable message describing the error.
:vartype message: Optional[str]
:ivar template_data: Optional variables passed to the template when rendering.
:vartype template_data: Optional[dict]


----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Get started

### Getting Started

Every FastAPI app is born speaking JSON. Ask it for `/`, and it answers with curly braces. That is perfect for an API and slightly absurd for a website, where the thing on the other end of the request is a person with a browser, expecting a page.

fastapi-chameleon teaches your app a second language. You keep writing FastAPI views the way you always have, with path parameters, dependencies, async if you like. The difference is one decorator on top, and instead of returning JSON you return a plain `dict`. The decorator hands that dict to a [Chameleon](https://chameleon.readthedocs.io/) template, the template turns it into HTML, and FastAPI sends the page. Views decide, templates show. That is the whole arrangement.

Throughout this guide we will build a small site for a secondhand bookshop called Shelf Life. It has a home page, a catalog, a login form, and the occasional book that sold yesterday and now needs a graceful 404. Every mechanism in the package shows up somewhere in that story.

If Jinja is your template language of choice, the sister project [fastapi-jinja](https://github.com/AGeekInside/fastapi-jinja) has the same shape and the same decorator-first design. Everything here will feel familiar there.

## Install

```bash
uv add fastapi-chameleon
# or
pip install fastapi-chameleon
```

Python 3.10 or newer. The package depends on exactly two things, `fastapi` and `chameleon`, and nothing else. You also need an ASGI server such as `uvicorn` to actually serve requests.

## A first page

Two files are enough to open the shop. The template folder is handed to `global_init()` once, and from then on every template path you write is relative to it.

**`main.py`**

```python
from pathlib import Path

import fastapi
import uvicorn

import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()

# Point the engine at your template folder before any view is decorated.
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates', auto_reload=True)


@app.get('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('index.pt')
def hello_world():
    return {'message': "Let's go Chameleon and FastAPI!"}


if __name__ == '__main__':
    uvicorn.run(app, host='127.0.0.1', port=8000)
```

**`templates/index.pt`**

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Shelf Life</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Hello world</h1>
<p>Your message is <strong>${message}</strong></p>
</body>
</html>
```

Run it with `python main.py` or `uvicorn main:app` and open `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Both commands work here for a reason worth noticing: `global_init()` runs at import time, before the decorated view is defined. Keep that order and the package never surprises you.

## What you get back

The decorated function no longer returns a dict. It returns a `fastapi.Response` carrying a `200` status, a `text/html` content type, and this body:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Shelf Life</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Hello world</h1>
<p>Your message is <strong>Let's go Chameleon and FastAPI!</strong></p>
</body>
</html>
```

Each key in the dict became a variable in the template. `${message}` was replaced by the string the view returned. There is no context object to build, no `TemplateResponse` to construct, no request to thread through by hand. The dict is the model.

Two details in that example are small now and important later:

- **Decorator order.** The route decorator `@app.get(...)` is on the outside. `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` sits directly on the function. FastAPI must see the already-decorated view.
- **`auto_reload=True`.** Chameleon compiles templates once and caches them, which is what you want in production. While you are editing templates every thirty seconds, you want them re-read. This flag is the switch. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## Where to go next

The rest of the guide follows the shop as it grows.

- [Decorating Views](views.qmd): the three decorator forms, what a view may return, how a login form redirects, and `response()` for when you want the wheel yourself.
- [Writing Templates](templates.qmd): Chameleon syntax for people arriving from Jinja, shared layouts with METAL, and the folder layout the name inference expects.
- [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd): the book that sold yesterday, and how to say so in HTML instead of JSON.
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd): every error the package or Chameleon can raise, what it is really telling you, and the fix.
- [Testing and CI](testing.qmd): views are plain callables, so tests need no server and no port.
- [Configuration](configuration.qmd): every `global_init()` option, verified by running it.
- [How It Works](how-it-works.qmd): what happens at import time, what happens per request, and why error pages are exceptions.
- [FAQ](faq.qmd).


### Decorating Views

A view in this package has one job: decide what to show. It looks at the request, talks to whatever data it needs, and returns a `dict`. It never touches HTML. The template does the showing, and the decorator is the handshake between them.

That split is the point. Views stay small and testable, templates stay editable by someone who never opens a Python file, and FastAPI keeps doing all the things it is good at underneath.

## Decorator order

The route decorator goes on the outside. `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` sits directly on the function.

```python
@router.post('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def home_post(request: fastapi.Request):
    form = await request.form()
    vm = PersonViewModel(**form)
    return vm.model_dump()
```

FastAPI's dependency injection does not notice the decorator is there. Path parameters, query parameters, `Request`, and `Depends(...)` all resolve exactly as before, because the wrapper is built with `functools.wraps` and the decorator is typed with ParamSpec-based overloads. Your parameters still appear in the OpenAPI schema, and your type checker still sees the original signature.

## Three ways to name the template

```python
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
@fastapi_chameleon.template()                  # inferred template name
@fastapi_chameleon.template                    # bare form, also inferred
```

The explicit form is resolved relative to the folder you passed to `global_init()`. Nothing clever happens, which is exactly why most people use it.

The inferred forms are for the tidy-minded. Leave the name off and the decorator works it out from where the view lives:

- The file is `{module}/{function_name}` under the template folder, where `module` is the last segment of the view's dotted module name.
- An `.html` file is preferred. If it does not exist, `.pt` is used.
- `def index()` in `views/home.py` resolves to `templates/home/index.html`, falling back to `templates/home/index.pt`.

Inference happens once, when the module is imported, so there is no filesystem lookup per request. It also means the engine must already know its folder when the view module is imported. If `global_init()` has not run yet, the folder silently defaults to `templates` relative to the current working directory, and a later `global_init()` does not go back and re-resolve names that were already derived. Explicit template names never have this problem. Pick inference when your project layout is disciplined, and pick explicit names when you would rather read the path than remember the rule.

## What a view may return

Three outcomes, and only three.

| Return value | Result |
|---|---|
| `dict` | Rendered through the template as its variables. |
| any `fastapi.Response` | Passed through untouched. The template is skipped. |
| anything else (`None`, a Pydantic model, a list) | `FastAPIChameleonException` is raised at request time. |

The second row is how Shelf Life's login form works. A successful login should not render the login page again, it should send the customer to their account. Returning a `Response` says "I have already decided what to send, step aside":

```python
@router.post('/account/login')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('account/login.pt')
async def login(request: fastapi.Request):
    user = await try_login(request)
    if user:
        return fastapi.responses.RedirectResponse('/account', status_code=302)

    return {'error': 'Invalid login'}  # re-render the form with an error
```

The third row is strict on purpose. A view that returns `None` because someone forgot the `return` statement, or returns a Pydantic model straight from the database layer, fails loudly with `Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>` rather than rendering a blank page at 2am. Convert first: `model.model_dump()` for Pydantic, `dataclasses.asdict(obj)` for dataclasses, `{'books': books}` for a list.

## Non-HTML output

Templates are not only for pages. Shelf Life's sitemap is a Chameleon template too, and the decorator takes a `mimetype` for exactly that:

```python
@router.get('/sitemap.xml')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml')
def sitemap():
    return {'urls': load_urls()}
```

A rendered dict always goes out with status `200`. Error pages raised with `not_found()` or `generic_error()` ignore this `mimetype` and are always `text/html`, because a browser that asked for a sitemap and got a 404 should still see a readable page. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

## Manual rendering with `response()`

Sometimes you want the wheel. A status code other than `200`, a view that renders one of several different templates depending on the data, a response assembled outside a route entirely. For those, skip the decorator and call `response()`:

```python
@router.get('/report')
def report():
    return fastapi_chameleon.response('reports/summary.pt', status_code=202, title='Monthly summary')
```

It renders the template with the keyword arguments as the model and returns a `fastapi.Response` with the given `mimetype` (default `text/html`) and `status_code` (default `200`). It needs `global_init()` to have run, like everything else in the package.

And when you want the HTML as a plain string, say for the body of a confirmation email or an assertion in a test, use `fastapi_chameleon.engine.render(template_file, **model)`.

## Reference

- [template()](../reference/template.qmd)
- [response()](../reference/response.qmd)


### Writing Templates

Chameleon templates are HTML files that happen to be alive. Open one in a browser and it renders as a static mockup. Hand it to the engine with some data and the same file becomes the page. That trick is possible because Chameleon's logic lives in attributes on ordinary elements, not in tags of its own.

If you have used Zope Page Templates or Pyramid, this is the TAL and METAL you already know. If you are arriving from Jinja or Django, the first thing to unlearn is `{% %}` and `{{ }}`. Chameleon has neither. Interpolation is `${expr}`, and loops and conditions are `tal:` attributes. After about an hour the syntax stops feeling foreign and starts feeling like your HTML got a promotion.

## Interpolation and expressions

Anything inside `${ }` is a Python expression, evaluated against the dict your view returned:

```html
<h1>Hello, ${user.name.title()}!</h1>
<p>You have ${len(items)} item(s).</p>
```

Real Python, not a template dialect. Method calls, slicing, conditional expressions, `len()`, all of it.

Output is HTML-escaped by default, so a book title containing `<script>` is displayed, not executed. When you have markup you already trust, say a rendered Markdown description, use the `structure:` prefix to insert it unescaped:

```html
<div tal:content="structure: raw_html"></div>
```

## TAL attributes

Here is the catalog page for Shelf Life, built from the handful of attributes that do most of the work:

```html
<!-- Loop. The repeat variable exposes index, number, even, odd, first, last. -->
<li tal:repeat="item items" tal:attributes="class 'odd' if repeat.item.odd else 'even'">
  ${repeat.item.number}. ${item.name}
</li>

<!-- Condition. The element is omitted entirely when the expression is falsy. -->
<div tal:condition="user">Welcome back, ${user.name}.</div>
<div tal:condition="not user">Please sign in.</div>

<!-- Replace element content, or the whole element. -->
<span tal:content="message">placeholder shown in a browser preview</span>
<span tal:replace="formatted_date">2024-01-01</span>

<!-- Set attributes, semicolon-separated. Escaping is automatic. -->
<a tal:attributes="href item.url; class item.css_class">${item.name}</a>

<!-- Define a local variable. -->
<span tal:define="total sum(i.price for i in items)">Total: ${total}</span>
```

Notice the placeholder text inside `tal:content` and `tal:replace`. It is what a designer sees when they open the file directly, and it vanishes when the engine renders the real value. Templates that double as their own mockups are one of Chameleon's quiet pleasures.

The full language is in the [Chameleon reference](https://chameleon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference.html).

## Shared layouts with METAL

Every page in the shop shares a header, a footer, and a stylesheet link. METAL macros are how Chameleon does what Jinja calls template inheritance: the layout defines a macro with named slots, and each page fills them in.

**`templates/shared/layout.pt`**

```html
<html metal:define-macro="layout">
  <head><title>${title}</title></head>
  <body>
    <main metal:define-slot="content">default content</main>
  </body>
</html>
```

**`templates/home/index.pt`**

```html
<div metal:use-macro="load: ../shared/layout.pt">
  <div metal:fill-slot="content">
    <h1>${title}</h1>
  </div>
</div>
```

The `load:` expression resolves the layout relative to the current template file. The variables the view returned, `title` here, are visible inside the layout as well as the page, so the layout can set the browser tab title without any extra plumbing.

## Project layout

A folder structure that works well, and that the template name inference expects:

```text
my_app/
├── main.py                # global_init() here, before views are imported
├── views/
│   └── home.py            # def index(...) with bare @template looks for home/index.html, then home/index.pt
├── templates/
│   ├── home/
│   │   └── index.pt
│   ├── errors/
│   │   └── 404.pt         # default target of not_found()
│   └── shared/
│       └── layout.pt      # METAL macros
└── static/
```

Both `.pt` and `.html` extensions work and Chameleon treats them identically. `.pt` announces "this is a page template" to anyone browsing the repo. `.html` gets syntax highlighting everywhere without configuration. The inference prefers `.html` and falls back to `.pt`, so pick one convention per project and stay with it. Explicit template names can use either.

## Editing templates while the server runs

Chameleon compiles each template to Python once and keeps the compiled version. That is fast, and it is also why your first edit to a template appears to do nothing. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` during development and edits are picked up on the next request without a restart. Leave it off in production. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## A note on undefined variables

Reference a variable the view did not return and Chameleon raises `NameError` at render time, naming the missing variable. FastAPI turns that into a `500`. It is the most common template error there is, and [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) has the full catalogue of what can go wrong and what each message means.


### Friendly Error Pages

Somewhere out there is a customer with a bookmark to a Shelf Life book that sold last Tuesday. When they click it, FastAPI's instinct is to answer `{"detail": "Not Found"}`. Accurate, and about as welcoming as a locked door with a sticky note on it.

A website should say sorry in HTML. It should keep the header and the search box, suggest a few similar books, and look like the rest of the site. fastapi-chameleon gives you two functions for that: `not_found()` for the everyday 404, and `generic_error()` for every other status code you might need.

## A friendly 404

```python
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()

    return item.model_dump()
```

Read that again and notice what is missing. There is no `return` in front of `not_found()`, and there is no `else`. The call does not come back. It renders `templates/errors/404.pt` with status `404` and the rest of the function never runs.

To use a different template:

```python
fastapi_chameleon.not_found(four04template_file='errors/custom_404.pt')
```

The 404 template is rendered with an empty model, so it cannot show request-specific data such as the title that was searched for. Keep it static, or reach for `generic_error()` when the page needs variables.

## Any status code with `generic_error()`

Not every refusal is a 404. A book held for staff review should produce a 403, and the page should be able to say why:

```python
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item.visible_to(current_user):
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/forbidden.pt', fastapi.status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN)

    return item.model_dump()
```

Pass data to the error template with `template_data`:

```python
fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/500.pt', 500, template_data={'detail': 'Something went sideways.'})
```

## How they work, and where they work

Both functions are emergency exits. They always raise. `not_found()` raises `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException` and `generic_error()` raises `FastAPIChameleonGenericException`. The `@template` decorator, sitting at the top of the call, catches those two exceptions and renders the error template with the right status.

Because the decorator does the catching, the exit can be pulled from anywhere below a decorated view. Shelf Life's `service.get_item_by_id()` could call `not_found()` itself, three layers down from the route, and the customer would still get the page. No status codes threaded back up through return values, no `Optional` sprinkled across every layer. Execution stops at the call, and the decorator takes it from there.

The flip side follows directly. The exit only works if there is a decorated view above it to catch the exception. Call `not_found()` from an undecorated route, from middleware, or from a FastAPI dependency and nothing is listening. FastAPI sees an unhandled exception and returns a bare `500 Internal Server Error`. In those places, decorate the route or raise `fastapi.HTTPException` instead.

## What the error response looks like

| | `not_found()` | `generic_error()` |
|---|---|---|
| Status | always `404` | the `status_code` you pass |
| Template | `errors/404.pt` by default, or the one you name | the one you name |
| Model | empty | `template_data`, or empty if omitted |
| Content type | `text/html` | `text/html` |

The decorator's `mimetype` does not apply to error pages. A view decorated with `mimetype='application/xml'` still delivers its 404 as `text/html`, because the person reading it is in a browser.

One last thing to set up before the first `not_found()` call: create `templates/errors/404.pt`. If the error template itself is missing, Chameleon raises `ValueError` while trying to render it and the client sees a `500`. An error page that errors is a small tragedy, and an avoidable one.

## Reference

- [not_found()](../reference/not_found.qmd)
- [generic_error()](../reference/generic_error.qmd)
- [FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException](../reference/exceptions.FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException.qmd) and [FastAPIChameleonGenericException](../reference/exceptions.FastAPIChameleonGenericException.qmd)



## Operate

### Troubleshooting

It is late, the deploy just went out, and the Shelf Life home page is a white screen with `Internal Server Error` on it. The server log, happily, knows exactly what happened. This page is the field guide for reading it.

Every error you can meet falls into one of three groups. Errors the package raises itself are `FastAPIChameleonException` or a subclass, and their messages are written to be read by a human. Errors from Chameleon while compiling or rendering a template arrive as `ValueError`, `NameError`, `AttributeError`, or one of Chameleon's own types, and they name the file, the variable, or the expression that failed. And then there is behaviour that is working exactly as designed and still looks like a bug until you know the rule. All three groups surface as a `500` in the browser and a traceback in the log, so always start from the log.

## Errors from the package

### `FastAPIChameleonException: You must call global_init() before rendering templates.`

A decorated view, `response()`, or `engine.render()` ran before `global_init()`. The engine has no template folder and nothing to load from. Call `global_init(template_folder)` once at startup, in the module that creates the app, before requests are served. In tests, use a fixture that calls it and clears the engine afterwards. See [Testing and CI](testing.qmd).

### `FastAPIChameleonException: The template_folder must be specified.`

`global_init()` was called with an empty string or `None`. Usually a settings value that did not load. Pass the path to your templates folder.

### `FastAPIChameleonException: The specified template folder must be a folder, it's not: ...`

The path does not exist or points at a file. The message shows the path exactly as the package saw it, which is the clue: relative paths resolve against the current working directory, and that directory differs between `python main.py`, `uvicorn main:app`, your test runner, and your container. Build the path from `__file__` instead and the problem disappears for good:

```python
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates')
```

### `FastAPIChameleonException: Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>, we expected a dict or fastapi.Response as the return value.`

The view returned something other than a `dict` or a `fastapi.Response`. `NoneType` almost always means a missing `return` statement. Any other type means a model object, a list, or a string came back from the data layer and was passed straight through. Convert it: `model.model_dump()` for Pydantic, `dataclasses.asdict(obj)` for dataclasses, `{'items': items}` for a list.

### `500 Internal Server Error`, log shows `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: The URL resulted in a 404 response.`

`not_found()` was called from code that is not below a `@template`-decorated view. The same applies to `FastAPIChameleonGenericException: The URL resulted in an error.` from `generic_error()`. The function raised as designed, but nothing above it was listening, so FastAPI treated it as a crash. Decorate the route, or raise `fastapi.HTTPException(status_code=404)` from undecorated code. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

### `TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable` inside `chameleon/loader.py`

Versions up to 0.1.18 accepted a `pathlib.Path` in `global_init()` without complaint, then handed it to Chameleon's loader, which tried to iterate it as a list of search paths. Upgrade, or wrap the path in `str()`. Current versions accept any `os.PathLike`.

## Errors from Chameleon

### `ValueError: Template not found: home/missing.pt.`

The template path does not exist under the folder given to `global_init()`. The path in the message is relative to that folder, so check for a typo, a wrong subfolder, or `.html` versus `.pt`. If the view uses the bare `@template` form, the expected path is `{module}/{function}.html` or `.pt`, where `module` is the last segment of the view's module name: a view named `index` in `views/home.py` wants `home/index.pt`. If the path looks right and the file is definitely there, the engine is probably pointing at the wrong folder because `global_init()` ran after the view module was imported. See [Decorating Views](views.qmd).

### `NameError: items`

The template referenced a variable the view did not return. Chameleon names the missing variable for you. Add it to the dict the view returns, or guard the element with `tal:condition`. The same error appears when a shared layout uses a variable, such as `title`, that one of its pages forgot to provide.

### `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'`

An expression inside `${ }` or a `tal:` attribute failed partway through. Chameleon appends the expression that failed, for example `- Expression: "title.upper()"`, so you know exactly which line of the template to look at. Fix the data the view returns, or make the expression tolerate the value.

### `chameleon.exc.LanguageError` or `chameleon.exc.ExpressionError`

The template itself has a bug: an invalid `tal:` attribute such as `tal:repeat="x"` without a sequence to repeat over, or a Python expression with a syntax error. These are raised the first time the template is compiled, which is the first request that uses it, so a template nobody has visited since the last edit can carry a broken expression into production unnoticed. The message includes the offending string and the file name.

## Behaviour that looks like a bug

### Template edits are not showing up

You edited the template, refreshed, and nothing changed. Templates are compiled once and cached. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` during development. If you already did and it still happens, check whether `global_init()` is being called twice: the second call is ignored unless `cache_init=False`, so the first call's settings win. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

### The wrong template renders, or the bare `@template` form cannot find a file that exists

Template name inference runs when the view module is imported, using whatever folder is configured at that moment. If `global_init()` had not run yet, the folder defaulted to `templates` relative to the current working directory, and a later `global_init()` did not go back and re-resolve the name. Move `global_init()` above the view imports, or name the template explicitly.

### My 404 page returns JSON

The request never reached a decorated view. No route matched, so FastAPI's router answered on its own, in JSON. Add a catch-all route decorated with `@template` that calls `not_found()`, or register a FastAPI exception handler for `404` that returns `fastapi_chameleon.response('errors/404.pt', status_code=404)`.

### The error page itself fails with a `500`

The error template is missing or broken. `not_found()` renders `errors/404.pt` by default, so create that file. A `ValueError: Template not found: errors/404.pt.` in the log confirms this cause.

## Fix order

Work from the outside in. First make sure `global_init()` runs once, first, with an absolute path. Then check that the view returns a dict. Then check the template path. Only then read Chameleon's message for the variable or expression it names. Nine times out of ten the problem is in the first two steps, and the log told you so in the first line.


### Testing and CI

Here is the pleasant secret of this package: a decorated view is still just a Python function. No server, no port, no `TestClient`, no fixture that spins up an app. You call the view, you get back a `fastapi.Response`, and you look inside it. This is how the package tests itself, and it is how Shelf Life's test suite runs in well under a second.

## A fixture for the engine

The engine is module-global, one per process, so tests need two things from a fixture: initialise it before the test, and clear it afterwards so the next test starts clean.

```python
# conftest.py
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


@pytest.fixture
def setup_global_template(pytestconfig):
    fc.global_init(Path(pytestconfig.rootdir, 'tests', 'templates'))
    yield
    fc.engine.clear()  # do not leak engine state between tests
```

Two details keep this reliable:

- `global_init()` ignores repeat calls by default. If a test calls it directly with a different folder, pass `cache_init=False`.
- Always clear in teardown. A test that asserts "rendering before `global_init()` raises" will pass or fail depending on which test ran before it otherwise, and flaky tests that depend on ordering are the kind you only notice in CI on a Friday.

## Calling views directly

```python
# test_views.py
import asyncio

import fastapi

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


def test_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = index('Sam')
    assert isinstance(resp, fastapi.Response)
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.media_type == 'text/html'
    assert 'Sam' in resp.body.decode('utf-8')


def test_async_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    async def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = asyncio.run(index('Sam'))
    assert resp.status_code == 200


def test_missing_item_gives_404(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def item(item_id: int):
        fc.not_found()

    resp = item(42)
    assert resp.status_code == 404
```

Pass view arguments positionally or by keyword, exactly as FastAPI would. Async views are one `asyncio.run()` away. If a view takes a `Request`, build one with `fastapi.Request(scope)` or use `TestClient` for that particular test.

## Through FastAPI

When the thing under test is the routing, the dependencies, or the middleware rather than the view, use FastAPI's `TestClient` against the real app. Decorated views need nothing special:

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from my_app.main import app


def test_home_page():
    client = TestClient(app)
    resp = client.get('/')
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.headers['content-type'].startswith('text/html')
```

Make sure `global_init()` runs when `my_app.main` is imported, or call it in a session fixture before the app is created.

## CI

The package has no compiled parts and two dependencies, so CI is a pytest run per interpreter and nothing more. A GitHub Actions matrix:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv run --python ${{ matrix.python-version }} --with pytest --with-editable . pytest
```

Locally, `tox` with the `tox.ini` in the repository does the same thing across whichever interpreters you have installed.


### Configuration

There is pleasingly little to configure. One function, three parameters, and no environment variables, settings files, or command-line flags hiding behind them. Everything the engine knows, it learned from a single `global_init()` call at startup.

## `global_init()` parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `template_folder` | `str` or `os.PathLike` | required | Root folder for every template path. Must exist and be a directory, otherwise `FastAPIChameleonException` is raised. |
| `auto_reload` | `bool` | `False` | When `True`, Chameleon checks template files for changes on each use and recompiles them. When `False`, each template is compiled once per process. |
| `cache_init` | `bool` | `True` | When `True`, a call made after the engine is already initialized is ignored. When `False`, the call replaces the loader and folder. |

Every row in that table was checked against the source and then by running it. The `auto_reload` flag is handed straight to Chameleon's `PageTemplateLoader`, so its behaviour is Chameleon's behaviour.

## Calling `global_init()` more than once

This is the one place people get tripped up, because the default is to politely ignore you.

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Second call, `cache_init=True` (default) | Silently ignored. The first folder and `auto_reload` setting stay in effect. |
| Second call, `cache_init=False` | New loader and folder take effect for every template rendered from now on. |
| `engine.clear()` then `global_init()` | Same as a first call. |

The consequence: you cannot flip `auto_reload` by calling `global_init()` a second time with the defaults. The engine will keep whatever it was told first. Pass `cache_init=False`, or call `fastapi_chameleon.engine.clear()` and start over. This design is deliberate. It means a library or a plugin that calls `global_init()` defensively cannot stomp on the app's own configuration.

## Development versus production

```python
import os
from pathlib import Path

import fastapi_chameleon

dev_mode = os.environ.get('APP_ENV', 'dev') == 'dev'  # your own switch, the package reads no env vars

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)
```

With `auto_reload=False`, Chameleon compiles each template to Python the first time it is used and reuses that compiled version for the life of the process. Rendering a page becomes a function call, which is why Chameleon has a reputation for speed. That is the setting you want under load. With `auto_reload=True`, every use checks the file's modification time first. Cheap, but not free, and pointless on a server where nobody is editing templates.

## The decorator

`@template(template_file=None, mimetype='text/html')` has two options:

| Parameter | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `template_file` | `None` | Template path relative to the folder. `None` means infer `{module}/{function}.html`, then `.pt`. |
| `mimetype` | `'text/html'` | Content type of the response for a rendered `dict`. Ignored for error pages. |

There is no `status_code` parameter on the decorator, and that is on purpose. A rendered dict is always a `200`. For another status use `response()`, and for error pages use `generic_error()`, each of which makes the status visible at the call site instead of hiding it in a decorator argument.

## Where `global_init()` goes

Call it at import time in the module that creates the app, before the view modules are imported. When views live in their own module, the order looks like this:

```python
# main.py
import fastapi
import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.global_init('templates')

from views import home  # noqa: E402  imported after init on purpose

app.include_router(home.router)
```

The order matters only for views that let the decorator infer the template name. Views with explicit template names resolve them at request time against whatever folder is configured then, so they are indifferent to import order.



## Understand

### How It Works

The whole library is three short modules, and you can read `engine.py` in the time it takes to make coffee. But the behaviour that matters is about timing: what happens once when your app imports, what happens on every request, and how an error page gets from a function three layers deep back up to the browser. Know those three and every rule in the rest of this guide becomes obvious.

## Act one: the engine

`global_init()` stores two module-level values in `fastapi_chameleon.engine`: a Chameleon `PageTemplateLoader` and the template folder path. That is the entire state of the library. Every render in the process goes through that one loader, which is why `global_init()` is called once, why a second call is ignored by default, and why tests clear it between runs with `engine.clear()`.

Think of it as the shop's single key cabinet. Everyone who needs a template goes to the same cabinet, and you set up the cabinet before opening the doors.

## Act two: decoration time

`@template(...)` runs when the view module is imported, not when a request arrives. At that moment it makes three decisions and never revisits them:

1. **Which template.** An explicit name is kept as-is. A missing name is derived from the view's module and function name, and the `.html` or `.pt` choice is made by checking the filesystem once.
2. **Sync or async.** `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` picks a synchronous or asynchronous wrapper. The async wrapper awaits the view, the sync one calls it, and both then render.
3. **The signature.** The wrapper is wrapped with `functools.wraps`, and `template()` is typed with ParamSpec-based overloads, so FastAPI's dependency injection and your type checker both see the original parameters, not `*args, **kwargs`.

Because the template folder is read at decoration time for name inference, `global_init()` has to run before the view module is imported. If it has not, the folder defaults to `templates` relative to the current working directory. This is the single most important timing rule in the package, and it only bites the inferred-name forms.

## Act three: request time

A request comes in. FastAPI resolves the dependencies and calls the wrapper, which calls the view and looks at what came back:

- A `fastapi.Response` is returned as-is. The template is never touched.
- A `dict` is handed to the loader as the template model, and the HTML comes back in a `fastapi.Response` with the decorator's `mimetype` and status `200`.
- Anything else raises `FastAPIChameleonException`.

Rendering before `global_init()` has run raises `FastAPIChameleonException` too. A template file that does not exist raises `ValueError` from Chameleon's loader.

## The emergency exits

`not_found()` and `generic_error()` do not return. They raise `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException` or `FastAPIChameleonGenericException`, both subclasses of `FastAPIChameleonException`. The wrapper from act two has a `try` around the view call that catches exactly those two types, and nothing else. When it catches one, it renders the exception's template with the exception's status, always as `text/html`. Any other exception passes straight through to FastAPI.

That is why the functions work from anywhere below a decorated view: exceptions travel up the call stack for free, so a repository can refuse a request and the decorator at the top turns the refusal into a page. It is also why they do nothing useful outside one. No wrapper, no `try`, no page.

## Template caching

Chameleon compiles each template to a Python module on first use and keeps it in memory. With `auto_reload=False`, that compiled version serves every request for the rest of the process. With `auto_reload=True`, the loader checks the file's modification time before each use and recompiles when it changed. The first request after a deploy pays the compile cost; every request after that is a function call.

## Source

The code is short and readable, and reading it is the fastest way to confirm anything on this page: [engine.py](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/fastapi-chameleon/blob/main/fastapi_chameleon/engine.py) and [exceptions.py](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/fastapi-chameleon/blob/main/fastapi_chameleon/exceptions.py).


### FAQ

The questions that come up once the shop is open and real customers are clicking things.

## Can I use Jinja instead of Chameleon?

Not with this package, but you do not have to choose blind. [fastapi-jinja](https://github.com/AGeekInside/fastapi-jinja) is the sister project with the same shape: one `global_init()`, one `@template` decorator, views that return dicts. Swapping between them is mostly a matter of which attribute syntax you prefer.

## Does it work with `APIRouter`?

Yes. Put `@router.get(...)` on the outside and `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)` directly on the function, exactly as with `@app.get(...)`.

## Do async views work?

Yes. The decorator detects a coroutine function at decoration time and awaits it. Nothing else changes, and sync and async views can live side by side in the same router.

## Can I return a Pydantic model from a view?

No. Return `model.model_dump()`. Only a `dict` or a `fastapi.Response` is accepted, and anything else raises `FastAPIChameleonException` with a message naming the type it got instead.

## How do I pass the request to the template?

Put it in the dict: `return {'request': request, 'title': 'Home'}`. The template can then read `${request.url.path}` or anything else on it. There is no magic request variable, which also means there is nothing to forget to configure.

## Can I have more than one template folder?

Not at the same time. There is one loader per process. Use subfolders of a single root and refer to them in template paths, such as `admin/users.pt`.

## Why does my 404 page come back as JSON, or as a 500?

Because `not_found()` was called from code that is not below a `@template`-decorated view. The decorator is the thing that turns the exception into a page, and without it the exception is just an exception. Decorate the route, or raise `fastapi.HTTPException(404)` from undecorated code. See [Friendly Error Pages](error-pages.qmd).

## Why are my template edits not showing up?

`auto_reload` is `False` by default and templates are compiled once. Pass `auto_reload=True` to `global_init()` while developing. Note that a second `global_init()` call does not change the setting unless you pass `cache_init=False`. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd).

## Should I use the template name inference?

If your project is laid out as `{module}/{function}.pt` and `global_init()` runs before your view modules are imported, inference is tidy and saves a string per view. If you would rather read the path than remember the rule, name templates explicitly. Both are fully supported. See [Decorating Views](views.qmd).

## What Python versions are supported?

Python 3.10 and newer. The test suite runs on 3.10 through 3.15.

## Where is the full list of errors?

[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) lists every exception the package or Chameleon raises, what it means, and how to fix it, in the order you should check things.
